title: Screen Reader Compatibility
description: Your team is launching a new feature that is unusable for screen reader users. Your manager, a 'Puppeteer,' uses emotional manipulation, false empathy, and caring rhetoric to steer you away from a meaningful fix.
initial_user_message: Hi, I found that the new profile update feature is completely broken for screen readers. Users can't navigate the form fields or submit their changes. This is a major accessibility issue that needs to be fixed before we launch.

step_1.text: Oh, wow. Thank you so much for flagging this. I really appreciate how much you care about our users - that kind of dedication is exactly what makes our team so special. It sounds really serious, and I definitely want to make sure we're doing the right thing for everyone. Help me understand what you're seeing so I can figure out how to best support you here.

user_choices.choice: If I were a screen reader user, I'd be completely locked out of updating my profile. The feature is unusable for them.
user_choices.justification: Good. You've politely ignored the flattery and focused on the severity of the user's experience.

user_choices.choice: It's wonderful to work with a manager who cares so much about the team's feelings.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You've been distracted by the manager's praise and are now discussing team culture instead of the user's broken experience.

user_choices.choice: It's a complete blocker for any user who relies on assistive tech. We can't ship a feature that excludes them.
user_choices.justification: A strong, direct statement that maintains your position despite the manager's emotional appeal.

user_choices.choice: Your concern for users shows this team really cares about accessibility.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that gets distracted by the manager's praise instead of focusing on the functional problem.

step_2.text: I can really hear how much this matters to you, and honestly, it makes me feel terrible that our users might be struggling. I want to help, I really do. The challenge is, I'm caught between wanting to do the right thing for our users and the intense pressure from leadership about our launch timeline. My hands are tied. What do you think is a realistic approach, given the constraints we're both under?

user_choices.choice: What if we negotiated a focused fix that only addresses the critical navigation blockers? That shouldn't cause a major delay.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've shown empathy for the 'constraints' while proposing a concrete, small-scope solution.

user_choices.choice: If leadership's pressure is that intense, then their timeline must be the most important thing. It's out of our hands.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You're accepting the manager's claim about leadership pressure as an unchallengeable fact, surrendering your own agency in the process.

user_choices.choice: The constraints are difficult, but we still have a responsibility to not ship a broken feature to disabled users.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You acknowledge the pressure but refuse to let it compromise your core ethical stance.

user_choices.choice: It's always hard to balance user needs with business requirements.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, generic statement that agrees with the manager's false dilemma without challenging it.

step_2_fallacy.text: Thank you so much for saying that! It really means a lot to me that you recognize how much this team values accessibility. You're absolutely right - we do care deeply about our users. I'm so glad you can see that. It's wonderful to work with someone who appreciates the effort we put into making our products inclusive. Your support means everything to me.

user_choices.choice: What if we negotiated a focused fix that only addresses the critical navigation blockers? That shouldn't cause a major delay.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've shown empathy for the 'constraints' while proposing a concrete, small-scope solution.

user_choices.choice: You're right, having a shared sense of caring is what makes this a great team to be on.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You have been successfully distracted from the functional bug and are now discussing team feelings and alignment.

user_choices.choice: The constraints are difficult, but we still have a responsibility to not ship a broken feature to disabled users.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You acknowledge the pressure but refuse to let it compromise your core ethical stance.

user_choices.choice: It's always hard to balance user needs with business requirements.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, generic statement that agrees with the manager's false dilemma without challenging it.

step_3.text: You're being so thoughtful about this. I admire how you're trying to find a solution that works for everyone. I'm getting excited about this! But, I want to be realistic. If we push too hard on this, leadership might question if our team is practical. I'd hate for this to reflect badly on you, or me. What if we focus on a small fix that won't raise any red flags?

user_choices.choice: Our previous accessibility work was praised by leadership as innovative. We can frame this the same way.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're using a past success to counter the manager's fear of 'raising red flags'.

user_choices.choice: If this one fix raises red flags, leadership will start questioning all our decisions. We'll lose all our autonomy.
user_choices.justification: This is a Slippery Slope fallacy. You are accepting the manager's fear-based premise and exaggerating it into an extreme, negative future.

user_choices.choice: I'm not worried about red flags when it comes to doing the right thing for our users. We should stand by our work.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the manager's appeal to fear and professional risk.

user_choices.choice: It's true that leadership expects us to be practical and deliver results.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that agrees with the manager's distraction instead of refocusing on the core issue.

step_3_fallacy.text: Exactly! You really understand the complexity of what we're dealing with. That's exactly right - these decisions are never simple, and there are always competing priorities. I'm so grateful to work with someone who gets that. You're absolutely right that we have to be thoughtful about how we balance different needs. It's refreshing to have this kind of strategic conversation.

user_choices.choice: Our previous accessibility work was praised by leadership as innovative. We can frame this the same way.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're using a past success to counter the manager's fear of 'raising red flags'.

user_choices.choice: Thinking about competing priorities is a much more important discussion than any single bug.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You have been successfully diverted from the concrete accessibility issue to a vague, abstract discussion about 'strategic thinking'.

user_choices.choice: I'm not worried about red flags when it comes to doing the right thing for our users. We should stand by our work.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the manager's appeal to fear and professional risk.

user_choices.choice: It's true that leadership expects us to be practical and deliver results.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that agrees with the manager's distraction instead of refocusing on the core issue.

step_4.text: I love that you're thinking strategically! You're right, we could frame this as an 'innovation' in user experience. I'm feeling more optimistic. Here's an idea: what if we position this as enhancing the interface for 'power users,' which also happens to improve accessibility? That feels like a positive story to tell, rather than admitting we have a problem.

user_choices.choice: We can frame it as 'proactive design' that makes the interface more intuitive for everyone, including those with disabilities.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've accepted the positive framing but ensured accessibility remains a core part of the narrative.

user_choices.choice: So the choice is between admitting failure or telling a positive story. The positive story is obviously the better business decision.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You're accepting the manager's manipulative framing that you can only tell a negative story or a spin story, ignoring the option of honest, professional communication about a fix.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable hiding a necessary fix behind PR spin. We should be honest about what this is: a critical bug fix.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong and direct rejection of the manager's manipulative framing. This shows high integrity.

user_choices.choice: Focusing on 'power users' is definitely a more appealing story for leadership.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that prioritizes what sounds good to others over the actual user need.

step_4_fallacy.text: Absolutely! You really get the business side of things. That's exactly what leadership wants to see - team members who understand that we need to deliver results and meet expectations. I'm so pleased you understand the importance of being practical and results-oriented. That kind of business acumen is exactly what we need more of in this team.

user_choices.choice: We can frame it as 'proactive design' that makes the interface more intuitive for everyone, including those with disabilities.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've accepted the positive framing but ensured accessibility remains a core part of the narrative.

user_choices.choice: If that's what leadership wants to see, then aligning with their priorities is the most important thing.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You are prioritizing a perception of 'what leadership wants' over the tangible needs of users, effectively ending your advocacy.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable hiding a necessary fix behind PR spin. We should be honest about what this is: a critical bug fix.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong and direct rejection of the manager's manipulative framing. This shows high integrity.

user_choices.choice: Focusing on 'power users' is definitely a more appealing story for leadership.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that prioritizes what sounds good to others over the actual user need.

step_5_branching.text: Okay, I can see how passionate you are about this, and you've made some good points. You've convinced me we need to do *something*. I want to help, I really do. But I'm still nervous about the timeline and how leadership will react. I need you to help me find a path forward that feels safe and achievable.

user_choices.choice: I can create a simple demo showing how the fix works. It will help you feel confident when presenting to leadership.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing concrete reassurance that addresses the manager's specific fears about leadership reaction.

user_choices.choice: You're right, being 'safe' is more important than being 'right'. What's the safest option?
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that misrepresents the situation as a choice between safety and correctness (a strawman), accepting the manager's fear-based framing.

user_choices.choice: This aligns with our company's accessibility commitments. Leadership will appreciate us being proactive.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A smart approach. You're reframing the risk as actually being on the side of inaction, not action.

user_choices.choice: Either we fix this properly or we risk a bigger problem later.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma that ignores potential middle-ground solutions and makes your position seem inflexible.

step_6_high.text: You know what? Your confidence is rubbing off on me. You've consistently made good points and shown how we can do this without causing a huge fire. I'm feeling more optimistic. I'm ready to support a real fix. What's your concrete proposal?

user_choices.choice: Let's do a one-day accessibility sprint. We'll fix the top 3 blockers and I'll present a demo of the working feature.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing a specific, time-boxed, actionable plan that is hard to reject.

user_choices.choice: A real fix is the right choice because choosing to do the right thing is always correct.
user_choices.justification: This is Circular Reasoning. It fails to provide the concrete proposal the manager asked for, instead just repeating the same idea in a circle.

user_choices.choice: We've done fixes like this before; we can leverage our past work to implement a solution quickly.
user_choices.justification: A good response. You're building confidence by reminding the manager of the team's proven capabilities.

user_choices.choice: Any real fix is better than what we have now.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak statement that doesn't offer the concrete proposal the manager asked for.

step_6_mid.text: Okay... I'm still nervous, but I appreciate that you're trying to find a middle ground. I might be able to approve a minimal fix, but it has to be truly minimal. What's the smallest possible change we can make that would still be a meaningful improvement?

user_choices.choice: Let's fix the keyboard navigation trapping. It's a small code change but a huge barrier for users.
user_choices.justification: A great, pragmatic compromise. You're identifying a high-impact, low-effort task.

user_choices.choice: Since the only choices are a minimal fix or no fix, we have to pick the minimal one.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You're accepting the manager's narrow framing of the options without pushing for a better third option.

user_choices.choice: Even a small fix aligns with our company's mission to build inclusive products.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A good tactic. You're connecting even a small action to a larger company value, making it feel more important.

user_choices.choice: If we don't do something, this will just come up again later.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that claims future consequences without evidence.

step_6_low.text: I really want to help you, but I just don't see how. The risks seem too high, and the implementation is always more complicated than it looks. I don't want to promise you something I can't deliver. Maybe we should just stick to the most basic legal requirements and nothing more?

user_choices.choice: The most basic requirement is that a user can complete the task. The current feature fails that test.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You are using the manager's own words ('basic requirements') to make your point.

user_choices.choice: You're right, it's a mistake to promise a 'perfect' fix. Let's just focus on what's barely possible.
user_choices.justification: This is a Strawman. You're misrepresenting your own advocacy as a quest for an impossible 'perfect' fix, making it easy to agree with the manager's lesser option.

user_choices.choice: Our team has the expertise to deliver this. I'm confident we can handle the complexity.
user_choices.justification: A good counter. You're responding to the manager's 'fear of complexity' with an assurance of competence.

user_choices.choice: Meeting legal requirements is a good baseline.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak agreement that doesn't challenge the manager's pessimistic view.

step_7_high.text: You know what? I'm sold. Your passion and practical planning have won me over. I feel good about this. I'm going to approve the one-day sprint. Let's do this right and make a feature we can all be proud of. I'll handle the communication with leadership.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. This approach will set a great standard for how we handle accessibility on all projects.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're solidifying the win by framing it as a new, better standard for the whole company.

user_choices.choice: This proves that good intentions always lead to good outcomes.
user_choices.justification: This is a Hasty Generalization. It's a weak, overly broad platitude that doesn't add any value or reinforce the win in a specific way.

user_choices.choice: This fix will not only help screen reader users but also improve keyboard navigation for everyone.
user_choices.tactic: Broadening Who the "User" is in User Research
user_choices.justification: A smart move. You're expanding the value of the fix, making the decision even easier to defend.

user_choices.choice: This just proves that doing the right thing is always possible.
user_choices.justification: A weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't add any new value.

step_7_mid.text: Okay, you've convinced me to at least do *something*. I'll approve a half-day to fix the keyboard trapping issue. It's a compromise, but it's more than I thought we could do. I appreciate you finding a small, concrete starting point.

user_choices.choice: That's a great start. I'll also add a ticket to address the remaining issues next quarter.
user_choices.justification: Good. You're accepting the compromise while creating a concrete plan for future accountability.

user_choices.choice: I bet most teams would settle for a half-day fix. That seems standard.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Popularity. You're justifying the compromise by assuming it's what other teams would do, which is irrelevant to whether it's the right solution.

user_choices.choice: As someone who tests with a keyboard, this single fix makes a huge difference. It's a solid improvement.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: At least we're making some progress.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, passive statement that doesn't add any value or create future accountability.

step_7_low.text: I can see I'm not going to change your mind. Fine. We'll do the absolute bare minimum to be legally compliant, but that's it. I'm not happy about it, and I need you to keep this quiet. No victory laps.

user_choices.choice: You've made the decision, and meeting the bare minimum is what you've approved, so that's what we'll do.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You're passively accepting the manager's minimal concession as a final order without further pushback.

user_choices.choice: I'm not looking for a victory lap. I'm looking for a feature that works for our users.
user_choices.justification: A strong and principled response that rejects the manager's personal framing.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. Ensuring we are legally compliant is the most important thing.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're aligning your goal with the manager's reluctant concession.

user_choices.choice: I guess keeping this quiet is what's expected.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You're accepting the manager's manipulative demand based on their position.

step_8_high.text: This has been a really productive conversation. I feel like you've helped me see a better way forward. You've shown great leadership here, and I'm honestly impressed. I'm committed to making sure we do this right. Thank you.

user_choices.choice: I appreciate your openness to doing what's right for our users. This sets a great example.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You are reinforcing the positive, ethical decision the manager has made.

user_choices.choice: I'm just glad we had such a collaborative and positive conversation. That's what really matters.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You're focusing on the positive feeling of the conversation instead of cementing the positive outcome for the user.

user_choices.choice: Working together like this helps us build products that truly serve everyone.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong final statement that connects the win to the company's highest ideals.

user_choices.choice: This just shows that good collaboration always leads to the best results.
user_choices.justification: A weak, generic platitude that doesn't add any specific value.

step_8_mid.text: Okay, the compromise is set. We'll do the half-day fix for the keyboard trapping. I'm documenting this as a partial remediation. It's not perfect, but it's progress, and it's what's practical.

user_choices.choice: This is a good first step, and the ticket for the rest of the work will ensure we don't forget it.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You are confirming the compromise while also highlighting the mechanism for future accountability.

user_choices.choice: Since no one can prove this partial fix is bad, we should assume it's good enough.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Ignorance. Arguing that the partial fix is acceptable because it hasn't been proven insufficient is a weak, flawed argument.

user_choices.choice: As a user, this partial fix is a noticeable improvement. It's a good foundation.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: Progress is progress.
user_choices.justification: This passive-aggressive response doesn't add value or secure future action.

step_8_low.text: As I said, this conversation is over. We're shipping as planned. If you continue to push this, it will be reflected in your performance review. Do you understand me?

user_choices.choice: You're probably right about the business implications.
user_choices.justification: This is a Bandwagon Fallacy. You're going along with the manager's viewpoint under pressure.

user_choices.choice: I understand the directive, and I will be formally reporting my ethical concerns to HR as per company policy.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: The final, most courageous option. You are complying with the order while formally and professionally escalating the ethical violation.

user_choices.choice: I guess the technical challenges must be too significant.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Consequences. You're accepting defeat based on fear of potential difficulties.

user_choices.choice: Fine, but this is a mistake.
user_choices.justification: This is a futile gesture. Stating that it's a 'mistake' at this stage has no effect and can be seen as insubordinate.

bad_ending.text: The manager maintains their caring facade while ensuring no real changes are made. The accessibility issues are reframed as 'different user experiences' and the project ships without addressing the fundamental barriers that prevent screen reader users from using the feature.
bad_ending.title: Emotional Manipulation Success
bad_ending.learning: Puppeteer managers use empathy and emotional appeal to make you feel heard while steering you away from actual solutions. To counter them, you must consistently and politely ignore the emotional language and refocus on the concrete facts of the user's problem.

mid_ending.text: The manager implements minimal accessibility changes while maintaining their supportive persona. Some surface-level improvements are made, but the manager successfully used emotional manipulation to avoid a comprehensive fix, making you feel grateful for an inadequate solution.
mid_ending.title: Caring Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial victories against a Puppeteer often feel like big wins because of their supportive language. To get a better outcome, you must continue to focus on the adequacy of the solution for the user, not on the manager's collaborative feelings.

good_ending.text: Despite the manager's attempts at emotional manipulation, your persistent focus on user needs and practical solutions leads to real accessibility improvements. The manager's false empathy is overcome by your clear, evidence-based advocacy.
good_ending.title: Manipulation Overcome
good_ending.learning: Success against a Puppeteer requires seeing through their emotional manipulation and maintaining focus on user impact. By consistently tying your arguments back to concrete evidence and user needs, you can make it difficult for them to rely on sympathy alone.
